claims.text: Spin-polarized density functional theory can be used to predict a ferromagnetic ground state.
The ground-state magnetic configuration can be identified by comparing the total energies of different magnetic configurations.
A ferromagnetic configuration with lower total energy than competing configurations indicates that the ferromagnetic state is stable.
Introducing magnetic dopants or adjusting alloy composition can induce magnetic interactions in a material that initially lacks intrinsic magnetic ordering.
The atomic lattice and orbital hybridization mediate exchange interactions between magnetic dopants or magnetic atoms.
Spin-polarized DFT can evaluate the total energies of ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, and nonmagnetic spin arrangements.
A ferromagnetic state lower in energy than antiferromagnetic and nonmagnetic states implies that intrinsic interactions favor ferromagnetism.
The ferromagnetic configuration will have a lower DFT-calculated total energy than other magnetic arrangements.
Experimental magnetometry will confirm robust ferromagnetic behavior.
The undoped or nonmagnetically doped baseline does not exhibit significant magnetic ordering.
The prediction is expected to hold at moderate dopant concentrations when structural parameters are well controlled.
Highly disordered dopant distributions may cause deviations from the prediction.
Strong spin-orbit coupling may cause deviations from the prediction by significantly influencing the electronic structure.
Prediction precision depends on the choice of exchange-correlation functional and the treatment of dopant distributions.
Systematic errors in the simulation method may affect quantitative predictions.
SQUID magnetometry, including temperature-dependent magnetization and hysteresis measurements, can assess whether ferromagnetic ordering is present.
